name: Haisla
confidence_why: Janzen 2023 derives Haisla stress from syllable weight (leftmost long vowel, else leftmost full vowel, else the final syllable) and Baleno, Janzen & Yoder 2024 confirm it acoustically, with Bach 1990 and Wilson 1987 agreeing that stress is largely predictable apart from lexically accented suffixes, but Vink 1977 presents minimal pairs and calls stress phonemic, and the fullest description, Lincoln & Rath 1986, remains unchecked.

catalog_quote: This analysis shows that word-stress in this language is fully predictable. As in all other North Wakashan languages, there is a strong preference for assigning word-stress to the leftmost syllable. Complicating this, however, is the presence of long vowels in x̄a’iselak̓ala: /aa, uu, ii, ai, au/. ... I analyse this language as being moraic based, that is, syllables with morae attract stress. The underlying vowels /a, u, i/ are moraic (µ). A schwa vowel followed by a resonant syllable coda /ən., əm., əl., əy., əw./ are also moraic. Schwa alone as a syllable nucleus is not moraic at all. The leftmost of these are assigned word-stress. ... I treat long vowels as heavy syllables, or as bimoraic (µµ). ... In each case, the heavy syllable will supersede the more regular leftmost stress rule pervasive in North Wakashan languages. ... when there is more than one heavy syllable within the same …
readall_conflicts: The one listed work (Lincoln & Rath 1986) could not be opened, so no conflict can be stated for it. Among the Haisla sources already held by the project in our check folder (downloaded 2026-09-16, not part of this task's work list), Vink 1977 ('A Haisla phonology', ICSNL 12, sec. 0.5, printed p. 115) says stress on the first syllable 'can by no means be given as a general rule, as a considerable amount of the items in the lexicon has middle or final stress', i.e. treats placement as lexical; Wilson 1987 (BLS 13, p. 326) says Haisla stress/pitch 'is not nearly so regular' as Nootkan or Kwak'wala and that some speakers replace stress with a HLH pitch pattern in connected discourse; Baleno, Janzen & Yoder 2024 (ICSNL 59, pp. 14-15) reconcile these as an ordered system: lexically stressed suffixes first, otherwise leftmost heavy (bimoraic) syllable, otherwise leftmost moraic syllable, otherwise (no moraic syllable) the final syllable, noting that the earlier authors did not take phonemic vowel length into account. So the older 'unpredictable' descriptions versus the 2024 weight-based analysis is the only disagreement, and the 2024 paper explains it as an analytical gap rather than a factual one.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every segment of the deciding quote, domain quote and exceptions quote is verbatim in the Janzen 2023 PDF we hold at the stated pages (188, 189, 191, 192, 194-195, 196, 198). (2) Deciding source: an 11-pp ICSNL working paper (2023) devoted to Haisla stress from recent fieldwork; kind = phonology article. Against Glottolog's list (Lincoln & Rath 1986 phonology+dictionary 511 pp; Vink 1977 ICSNL sketch; Bach 2002 irrelevant) and the ICSNL archive (index through ICSNL 60/2025 checked), it is the best analysis of stress placement, and it now has an instrumental sequel: Baleno, Janzen & Yoder 2024 (ICSNL 59, downloaded) restates the identical ordered rules (lexical suffix > leftmost bimoraic > leftmost moraic > rightmost), reports pitch/duration/intensity as p<0.001 correlates, and says re-transcribing vowel length cut the exception list from 88 to 10 words. sources.citation: Baleno, Grace, Jonathan Janzen & Brendon Yoder. 2024. Acoustic Correlates of Word Stress in Haisla. In D. K. E. Reisinger et al. (eds.), Papers for ICSNL 59, 14-23. Vancouver: UBCWPL.
sources.quote: 'Haisla typically assigns stress like other North Wakashan languages to the leftmost stress-bearing (moraic) syllable, or applies the default-to-opposite rule if the word contains no moraic syllable... (1) Assign stress to a lexically stressed syllable. (2) Assign stress to the leftmost heavy (bimoraic) syllable. (3) If no syllable is bimoraic, assign stress to the leftmost moraic syllable. (4) If no syllable contains a mora, assign stress to the rightmost syllable.' sources.citation: Bach, Emmon. 1990. Stem extensions in Haisla. Papers for ICSNL 25, 1-15.
sources.quote: p.11: 'We know that the distinction between light and heavy syllables plays a role in the stress system of Kwakw'ala and probably in Haisla as well (Boas, 1947; Bach, 1975).' fn.2: 'the stress or accent systems of the other North Wakashan languages differ both from each other and from Kwakw'ala... It appears to me that Haisla has a system of accented and unaccented suffixes overlaid on a system perhaps of the same general sort as that posited for Kwakw'ala in Bach (1975).' (This is the passage Janzen 2023 quotes.)

sources.quote: 'Lincoln and Rath, in their study of Kwakiutlan roots, mention a dialect split in Haisla. While one group maintains the rough outlines of the historical system (stress sometimes accompanied by pharyngealization of the vowel), the other group uses stress only in words given in isolation. In connected discourse, stress is replaced by these speakers with a HLH pitch pattern on the accented syllable...
